claims.source: These neurons express lower levels of the stress sensor FoxO than neighboring epidermal cells, and hence exhibit no marked induction of autophagy and a milder suppression of Tor signaling under nutrient stress.
claims.evidence: This is supported by pRpS6 staining data showing Tor activity in neurons versus epidermal cells.

claims.claim: Preferential dendrite growth allows for heightened animal responses to sensory stimuli.
claims.source: Preferential dendrite growth allows for heightened animal responses to sensory stimuli, indicative of a potential survival advantage under environmental challenges.
claims.evidence: This is supported by behavioral assay data showing increased thermal nociception in larvae reared under nutrient restriction.

claims.claim: Brain sparing in human fetuses experiencing intrauterine growth restriction results in undersized newborns with disproportionately large heads.
claims.source: This phenomenon of 'organ sparing' is exemplified by the preferential growth of the brain in human fetuses experiencing intrauterine growth restriction, resulting in undersized newborns with disproportionately large heads (Gruenwald, 1963).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Gruenwald, 1963.

claims.claim: Changes of circulation enhance oxygen and blood supply towards the brain under nutrient deprivation in mammals.
claims.source: Although changes of circulation are known to enhance oxygen and blood supply towards the brain under nutrient deprivation in mammals (Severi et al., 2000; Cohen et al., 2015), how systemic growth control is altered at the molecular level to favor brain development remains poorly understood.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Severi et al., 2000 and Cohen et al., 2015.

claims.claim: Systemic larval body growth of Drosophila is controlled by the conserved insulin/insulin like growth factor (IGF) pathway.
claims.source: Systemic larval body growth of Drosophila is controlled by the conserved insulin/insulin like growth factor (IGF) pathway (Rulifson et al., 2002).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Rulifson et al., 2002.

claims.claim: Drosophila insulin-like peptides (Dilps) secreted by the insulin producing cells (IPCs) in the larval brain promote cell proliferation and growth of peripheral tissues by activating the insulin receptor (InR) and the downstream signaling components phosphatidylinositol 3-kinase (PI3K) and Akt (PKB).
claims.source: Drosophila insulin-like peptides (Dilps) secreted by the insulin producing cells (IPCs) in the larval brain promote cell proliferation and growth of peripheral tissues by activating the insulin receptor (InR) and the downstream signaling components phosphatidylinositol 3-kinase (PI3K) and Akt (PKB) (Verdu et al., 1999; Brogiolo et al., 2001; Ikeya et al., 2002; Oldham et al., 2002).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations.

claims.claim: Nutrient restriction suppresses insulin secretion through an intricate nutrient sensing mechanism involving inter-organ communications between the fat body and IPCs.
claims.source: Nutrient restriction suppresses insulin secretion through an intricate nutrient sensing mechanism involving inter-organ communications between the fat body and IPCs (Ikeya et al., 2002; Géminard et al., 2009; Rajan and Perrimon, 2012), and consequently, curbs the growth of most peripheral tissues.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Ikeya et al., 2002; Géminard et al., 2009; Rajan and Perrimon, 2012.

claims.claim: The larval brain is protected against nutrient deprivation and exhibits continuous neurogenesis.
claims.source: However, the larval brain is protected against nutrient deprivation and exhibits continuous neurogenesis (Cheng et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Cheng et al., 2011.

claims.claim: Brain protection during nutrient deprivation is mediated by the glia-derived Jelly belly (Jeb) ligand that activates the Anaplastic lymphoma kinase (Alk) receptor on neural stem cells (NSCs) to turn on the downstream PI3K pathway independent of nutrition.
claims.source: This protection is mediated by the glia-derived Jelly belly (Jeb) ligand that activates the Anaplastic lymphoma kinase (Alk) receptor on neural stem cells (NSCs) to turn on the downstream PI3K pathway independent of nutrition (Cheng et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Cheng et al., 2011.

claims.claim: The dendritic arbors of Drosophila somatosensory neurons called dendritic arborization (da) neurons are known to scale with the body wall during normal larval development.
claims.source: For example, the dendritic arbors of Drosophila somatosensory neurons called dendritic arborization (da) neurons are known to scale with the body wall during normal larval development (Parrish et al., 2009).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Parrish et al., 2009.

claims.claim: Dendritic scaling involves synchronous expansion of body wall epidermal cells and of da dendritic arbors, such that neurons maintain the same coverage of the sensory fields while the body surface area expands exponentially.
claims.source: This scaling involves synchronous expansion of body wall epidermal cells and of da dendritic arbors, such that neurons maintain the same coverage of the sensory fields while the body surface area expands exponentially (Jiang et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Jiang et al., 2014.

claims.claim: Da neurons are categorized into four classes that differ in their dendrite morphology and transcription factor expression.
claims.source: Da neurons are categorized into four classes that differ in their dendrite morphology and transcription factor expression (Grueber et al., 2002; Hattori et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Grueber et al., 2002 and Hattori et al., 2013.

claims.claim: Class IV da (C4da) neurons completely cover the body surface and are called 'space-filling' neurons.
claims.source: Recently, class IV da (C4da) neurons, which completely cover the body surface and thus are called 'space-filling' neurons (Grueber et al., 2002; Grueber et al., 2003), were found to elaborate more dendrite branches when larvae develop on a low-nutrient diet (Watanabe et al., 2017), suggesting that dendritic scaling of C4da neurons is regulated by the nutrient state.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Grueber et al., 2002 and Grueber et al., 2003.

claims.claim: C4da neurons were found to elaborate more dendrite branches when larvae develop on a low-nutrient diet.
claims.source: Recently, class IV da (C4da) neurons, which completely cover the body surface and thus are called 'space-filling' neurons (Grueber et al., 2002; Grueber et al., 2003), were found to elaborate more dendrite branches when larvae develop on a low-nutrient diet (Watanabe et al., 2017), suggesting that dendritic scaling of C4da neurons is regulated by the nutrient state.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Watanabe et al., 2017.

claims.claim: The conserved PI3K-Akt-mechanistic target of rapamycin (mTOR) pathway promotes dendrite growth in both insects and mammals.
claims.source: The conserved PI3K-Akt-mechanistic target of rapamycin (mTOR) pathway promotes dendrite growth in both insects and mammals (Jaworski et al., 2005; Kumar et al., 2005; Parrish et al., 2009; Skalecka et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations.

claims.claim: The PI3K-Akt-mTOR pathway enhances translation in most cells by mTOR kinase-mediated phosphorylation of S6 protein kinase (S6K) and 4E-binding protein (4E-BP).
claims.source: Receiving signaling inputs from membrane receptor tyrosine kinases (RTKs), notably InR (Sancak et al., 2007; Vander Haar et al., 2007; Wang et al., 2007), this pathway enhances translation in most cells by mTOR kinase-mediated phosphorylation of S6 protein kinase (S6K) and 4E-binding protein (4E-BP) (Burnett et al., 1998).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations.

claims.claim: mTOR activity is influenced by the cellular state, including nutrient availability, cellular energy levels, and stress factors.
claims.source: At the center of this pathway, mTOR activity is also influenced by the cellular state, including nutrient availability, cellular energy levels, and stress factors (Zoncu et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Zoncu et al., 2011.

claims.claim: Cellular nutrient starvation suppresses mTOR and consequently induces autophagy.
claims.source: In particular, cellular nutrient starvation suppresses mTOR and consequently induces autophagy (Ganley et al., 2009; Hosokawa et al., 2009; Jung et al., 2009), the self-eating process that helps to conserve and recycle vital cellular building blocks.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Ganley et al., 2009; Hosokawa et al., 2009; Jung et al., 2009.

claims.claim: mTOR regulates autophagy in part through the transcription factor EB (TFEB), which promotes autophagosome biogenesis but is suppressed by mTOR-mediated phosphorylation.
claims.source: mTOR regulates autophagy in part through the transcription factor EB (TFEB), which promotes autophagosome biogenesis but is suppressed by mTOR-mediated phosphorylation (Jung et al., 2009; Martina et al., 2012; Roczniak-Ferguson et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Jung et al., 2009; Martina et al., 2012; Roczniak-Ferguson et al., 2012.

claims.claim: The forkhead box O (FoxO) family of transcription factors can be activated by a variety of stress signals and respond by suppressing cell growth and inducing autophagy.
claims.source: Among the cellular stress sensors that inhibit mTOR activity, the forkhead box O (FoxO) family of transcription factors can be activated by a variety of stress signals and respond by suppressing cell growth and inducing autophagy (Eijkelenboom and Burgering, 2013).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Eijkelenboom and Burgering, 2013.

claims.claim: FoxO members have been found to enhance dendritic space-filling of C4da neurons in Drosophila.
claims.source: Furthermore, although FoxO members have been found to enhance dendritic space-filling of C4da neurons in Drosophila (Sears and Broihier, 2016) and to regulate dendrite branching and spine morphology of adult-generated neurons in mice (Schäffner et al., 2018), whether they also influence neuronal arbor growth in response to nutrient stress is unclear.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Sears and Broihier, 2016.

claims.claim: FoxO regulates dendrite branching and spine morphology of adult-generated neurons in mice.
claims.source: Furthermore, although FoxO members have been found to enhance dendritic space-filling of C4da neurons in Drosophila (Sears and Broihier, 2016) and to regulate dendrite branching and spine morphology of adult-generated neurons in mice (Schäffner et al., 2018), whether they also influence neuronal arbor growth in response to nutrient stress is unclear.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Schäffner et al., 2018.

claims.claim: C4da neurons in the HY condition showed sparse dendrites with gaps of dendritic coverage between neighboring neurons.
claims.source: In wandering third instar larvae, C4da neurons in the HY condition showed sparse dendrites with gaps of dendritic coverage between neighboring neurons (Figure 1A).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1A.

claims.claim: C4da neurons in the LY condition completely covered the body wall with dense dendrites.
claims.source: In contrast, C4da neurons in the LY condition completely covered the body wall with dense dendrites (Figure 1B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1B.

claims.claim: Apparent dendrite overgrowth in the LY condition was due to 60% more total branches and 59% more terminal branches but not increase of terminal branch length as compared to the HY condition.
claims.source: This apparent dendrite overgrowth in the LY condition (Figure 1D) was due to 60% more total branches and 59% more terminal branches but not increase of terminal branch length as compared to the HY condition (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: LY caused a significant delay in larval body growth, with animals in LY taking 2.2 times longer (264 hr compared to 120 hr) to pupariate.
claims.source: Compared to the HY condition, LY caused a significant delay in larval body growth, with animals in LY taking 2.2 times longer (264 hr compared to 120 hr) to pupariate.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations of developmental timing.

claims.claim: Larvae reared in HY and LY reached a nearly identical maximum segment width of ~600 μm before pupariation.
claims.source: Notably, larvae reared in HY and LY reached a nearly identical maximum segment width of ~600 μm before pupariation (Figure 1A–C).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1A-C.

claims.claim: C4da neurons grew slower in LY than in HY, as indicated by smaller increases of the total dendrite length during each 24 hr period.
claims.source: C4da neurons also grew slower in LY than in HY, as indicated by smaller increases of the total dendrite length during each 24 hr period (Figure 1D).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1D.

claims.claim: LY larvae ultimately had neurons that outgrew those of HY larvae, resulting in 1.39-fold longer total dendrites at the end of the larval period.
claims.source: However, because LY larvae had more time to develop, their neurons ultimately outgrew those of HY larvae, resulting in 1.39-fold longer total dendrites at the end of the larval period (Figure 1D).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1D.

claims.claim: C4da dendrites grow 57% faster in LY than in HY when normalized by the segment width.
claims.source: This plot shows that C4da dendrites grow 57% faster (based on the slopes of the linear fits) in LY than in HY when normalized by the segment width.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative analysis of dendrite growth data normalized to segment width.

claims.claim: The dendrite density was always higher in LY when plotted against the segment width.
claims.source: Interestingly, the dendrite density (dendrite length/dendrite field size) was always higher in LY when plotted against the segment width (Figure 1F), even though the dendrite length was not greater in LY when the segment width was below 200 μm (Figure 1E).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1F.

claims.claim: C4da neurons showed significant dendrite growth over a 24 hr period under starvation, even though the larval body size did not change in the same period.
claims.source: Interestingly, C4da neurons showed significant dendrite growth as measured by the dendrite length normalized to the segment width (abbreviated as normalized dendrite length) over a 24 hr period (Figure 1—figure supplement 3A), even though the larval body size did not change in the same period (Figure 1—figure supplement 3B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3A and 3B.

claims.claim: Downregulation of the InR/Tor pathway in neurons by InR knockdown, InRDN overexpression, Tor knockdown, or TorDN overexpression in the HY condition caused mild or statistically non-significant dendrite reduction compared to the control.
claims.source: Downregulation of the InR/Tor pathway in neurons by InR knockdown (InR RNAi), InRDN (dominant negative) overexpression (InR DN), Tor knockdown (Tor RNAi), or TorDN overexpression (Tor DN) in the HY condition caused mild or statistically non-significant dendrite reduction compared to the control (Figure 2A–C and G, and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–1C).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2A-C, G and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A-1C.

claims.claim: The same genetic manipulations that mildly affected dendrites in HY caused pronounced dendritic reduction in the LY condition, generating dendrite patterns resembling those of wildtype neurons in the HY condition.
claims.source: In contrast, the same genetic manipulations caused pronounced dendritic reduction in the LY condition, generating dendrite patterns resembling those of wildtype neurons in the HY condition (Figure 2D–F and G, and Figure 2—figure supplement 1D–1F).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2D-F, G and Figure 2—figure supplement 1D-1F.

claims.claim: Neuronal InR/Tor signaling is responsible for the preferential dendrite growth observed under nutrient stress.
claims.source: These results suggest that neuronal InR/Tor signaling is responsible for the preferential dendrite growth observed under nutrient stress.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the genetic manipulation experiments showing nutrient-dependent effects.

claims.claim: Epidermal Atg8a knockdown using Gal4R16D01 had no effect on cell size under the HY condition.
claims.source: Epidermal Atg8a knockdown using Gal4R16D01 had no effect on cell size under the HY condition (Figures 3D, E and H), consistent with the low autophagy level in these cells.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figures 3D, E and H.

claims.claim: Epidermal Atg8a knockdown caused a 16% increase of the epidermal cell size under LY.
claims.source: However, the same manipulation caused a 16% increase of the epidermal cell size under LY (Figure 3F and G, and 3H), supporting the idea that autophagy suppresses epidermal cell growth under nutrient stress.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3F, G and 3H.

claims.claim: Neuronal Atg8a knockdown in both HY and LY conditions resulted in similar increases of normalized dendrite length (13% and 11% increases, respectively).
claims.source: In comparison, neuronal Atg8a knockdown in both HY and LY conditions resulted in similar increases of normalized dendrite length (13% and 11% increases, respectively) (Figure 3I and Figure 3—figure supplement 2A–2D), suggesting that C4da neurons maintain a constant level of autophagy regardless of nutrient availability to mildly suppresses dendrite growth.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3I and Figure 3—figure supplement 2A-2D.

claims.claim: Mitf-GFPnls showed nutrient-independent expression in epidermal nuclei but its expression could not be detected in da neurons in either HY or LY condition.
claims.source: Mitf-GFPnls showed nutrient-independent expression in epidermal nuclei but its expression could not be detected in da neurons in either HY or LY condition (Figure 3—figure supplement 2E–G), suggesting that Mitf transcription may be low in da neurons.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2E-G.

claims.claim: Overexpression of Mitf in C4da neurons strongly reduced the normalized dendrite length under LY.
claims.source: We next investigated the effects of inducing autophagy on dendrite growth by overexpressing Mitf in C4da neurons, as overexpression of TFEB/Mitf is sufficient to dominantly induce autophagy in cells (Settembre et al., 2011; Zhang et al., 2015). This manipulation strongly reduced the normalized dendrite length under LY (Figure 3J–L), suggesting that high autophagy levels suppress dendrite growth.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3J-L.

claims.claim: FoxO-GFP was expressed at similar levels in epidermal cells in both HY and LY conditions.
claims.source: FoxO-GFP was expressed at similar levels in epidermal cells in both HY and LY conditions (Figure 4A–C) but could not be detected above the background noise level in C4da cell bodies (Figure 4A–C).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4A-C.

claims.claim: FoxO-GFP could not be detected above the background noise level in C4da cell bodies.
claims.source: FoxO-GFP was expressed at similar levels in epidermal cells in both HY and LY conditions (Figure 4A–C) but could not be detected above the background noise level in C4da cell bodies (Figure 4A–C).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4A-C.

claims.claim: Within 4 hr of starvation, FoxO-GFP was drastically enriched in epidermal nuclei.
claims.source: Within 4 hr of starvation, FoxO-GFP was drastically enriched in epidermal nuclei (Figure 4—figure supplement 2H and J).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2H and J.

claims.claim: FoxO-GFP remained undetectable in da neurons of 75% of larvae after 4 hr of starvation.
claims.source: In the same experiment, FoxO-GFP remained undetectable in da neurons of 75% of larvae (Figure 4—figure supplement 2H and J) but increased to moderate levels in nuclei of da neurons of the rest of larvae (Figure 4—figure supplement 2I and J).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2H and J.

claims.claim: foxo-Gal4 drove uniform epidermal expression of a UAS-tdTom reporter under HY, and the expression was enhanced 2.9 folds by nutrient stress.
claims.source: This foxo-Gal4 drove uniform epidermal expression of a UAS-tdTom reporter under HY, and the expression was enhanced 2.9 folds by nutrient stress (Figure 4E–G).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4E-G.

claims.claim: foxo-Gal4 showed minimal activity in C4da neurons under both HY and LY conditions.
claims.source: In contrast, foxo-Gal4 showed minimal activity in C4da neurons under both HY and LY conditions (Figure 4E–G), confirming the results obtained by FoxO-GFP and FoxO staining.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4E-G.

claims.claim: Knocking down foxo in C4da neurons had no effect on normalized dendrite length in either HY or LY condition.
claims.source: We found that knocking down foxo in C4da neurons had no effect on normalized dendrite length in either condition (Figures 4H, I, K, L and N), but caused 13% reduction of dendrite density in LY medium.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figures 4H, I, K, L and N.

claims.claim: Overexpressing FoxO in C4da neurons caused mild (11.7%) and strong (49.2%) reduction of normalized dendrite length in HY and LY conditions, respectively.
claims.source: On the other hand, overexpressing FoxO in C4da neurons caused mild (11.7%) and strong (49.2%) reduction of normalized dendrite length in HY and LY conditions, respectively (Figures 4J, M and N).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figures 4J, M and N.

claims.claim: Knocking down foxo in epidermal cells had no effect in HY but increased the epidermal cell size by 34% under the LY condition.
claims.source: Lastly, we examined the role of FoxO in epidermal cell growth by knocking down foxo using Gal4R16D01. The knockdown had no effect in HY but increased the epidermal cell size by 34% under the LY condition (Figure 4O–S).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4O-S.

claims.claim: In HY, neuronal FoxO overexpression did not cause detectable changes in the ratio of pRpS6 levels between neuronal compartments and epidermal cells.
claims.source: In HY, neuronal FoxO overexpression did not cause detectable changes in the ratio of pRpS6 levels between neuronal compartments and epidermal cells (Figures 2M, 5A, C and D).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figures 2M, 5A, C and D.

claims.claim: In LY, while pRpS6 levels in the somas of FoxO-overexpressing neurons were still higher than in epidermal cells, the dendritic pRpS6 signal was reduced to levels lower than those of epidermal cells.
claims.source: However, in LY, while pRpS6 levels in the somas of FoxO-overexpressing neurons were still higher than in epidermal cells, the dendritic pRpS6 signal was reduced to levels lower than those of epidermal cells (Figure 5B–D).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5B-D.

claims.claim: While the autophagosome level in C4da cell bodies was not altered by FoxO-expression in HY, it increased 4.9 folds in LY.
claims.source: We further examined the autophagy level of FoxO-overexpressing neurons using mCherry-Atg8a, as higher autophagy levels suppress the growth of both C4da neurons and epidermal cells (Figure 3). While the autophagosome level in C4da cell bodies was not altered by FoxO-expression in HY, it increased 4.9 folds in LY (Figure 4E–G).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4E-G (note: this appears to be a typo in the manuscript, should be Figure 5E-G based on context).

claims.claim: Over a range of temperatures (from 40°C to 46°C), a larger percentage of LY larvae exhibited nocifensive rolling responses to thermal stimuli than HY larvae.
claims.source: Over a range of temperatures (from 40°C to 46°C), we found that a larger percentage of LY larvae exhibited nocifensive rolling responses to thermal stimuli than HY larvae (Figure 6A).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 6A.

claims.claim: The temperatures required to induce response in a similar percentage of larvae were approximately 2°C lower for the LY condition than for the HY condition.
claims.source: The temperatures required to induce response in a similar percentage of larvae were approximately 2°C lower for the LY condition than for the HY condition.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of behavioral data.

claims.claim: Significantly more larvae in LY responded within 5 s (fast response) of heat stimulus over a temperature range from 43°C to 48°C.
claims.source: We additionally monitored response latency and found that significantly more larvae in LY responded within 5 s (fast response) of heat stimulus over a temperature range from 43°C to 48°C (Figure 6B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 6B.

claims.claim: FoxO overexpression in C4da neurons significantly reduced the percentages of LY larvae that showed fast responses and overall response at 46°C.
claims.source: While FoxO overexpression did not significantly change the rolling behaviors of HY larvae, it significantly reduced the percentages of LY larvae that showed fast responses and overall response (Figure 6D and E).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 6D and E.

claims.claim: The yeast concentration did not have obvious effects on the total dendrite length of C1da neuron ddaE.
claims.source: Consistent with the previous report by Watanabe et al., 2017, we found that the yeast concentration did not have obvious effects on the total dendrite length of C1da neuron ddaE (Figure 7A–C).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 7A-C and is consistent with a prior report.

claims.claim: Nutrient stress stimulated the dendritic growth of C3da neurons ddaA and ddaF: the total dendrite length increased by 40% and 32%, respectively; the total terminal dendrite length increased by 61% and 46%, respectively; the terminal branch numbers increased by 47% and 58%, respectively.
claims.source: However, nutrient stress stimulated the dendritic growth of C3da neurons ddaA and ddaF: the total dendrite length increased by 40% and 32%, respectively; the total terminal dendrite length increased by 61% and 46%, respectively; the terminal branch numbers increased by 47% and 58%, respectively (Figure 7D–H).

claims.claim: The cell bodies of C1da and C3da neurons showed variable and cell-specific baseline autophagy levels in HY, but these levels did not appear to be altered by the nutrient level.

claims.evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 7I-M.

claims.claim: C1 ddaE neurons showed a much higher level of the lysosomal marker Lamp-mCherry than other da classes in HY, and this level was enhanced 2.7 folds by nutrient stress.
claims.source: Interestingly, C1 ddaE neurons showed a much higher level of the lysosomal marker Lamp-mCherry than other da classes in HY, and this level was enhanced 2.7 folds by nutrient stress (Figures 7N, P and R), suggesting that C1da neurons have uniquely high and nutrient-dependent lysosomal system.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figures 7N, P and R.

claims.claim: C1da and C3da neurons showed only background-noise levels of FoxO-GFP and foxo>tdTom signals.
claims.source: Lastly, we examined foxo expression in C1da and C3da neurons using foxo-GFP and foxo-Gal4. Similar to C4da neurons, C1da and C3da neurons showed only background-noise levels of FoxO-GFP and foxo >tdTom signals (Figure 7M and N).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 7M and N.

claims.claim: C4da neurons are polymodal nociceptive neurons that respond to noxious thermal, mechanical, chemical, and light stimuli.

claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Tracey et al., 2003; Hwang et al., 2007; Xiang et al., 2010.

claims.claim: The preferential dendrite growth of da neurons constitutes another form of nervous system sparing that bears important distinctions from Drosophila brain sparing.
claims.source: The preferential dendrite growth of da neurons constitutes another form of nervous system sparing that bears important distinctions from Drosophila brain sparing.
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation of the study's findings in the context of known brain sparing mechanisms.

claims.claim: While proliferating neural stem cells in the CNS is protected against starvation, individual post-mitotic da neurons are spared at the level of neuronal arbor growth.
claims.source: First, while proliferating neural stem cells in the CNS is protected against starvation (Cheng et al., 2011), individual post-mitotic da neurons are spared at the level of neuronal arbor growth.
claims.evidence: This claim contrasts the current findings with prior work cited (Cheng et al., 2011).

claims.claim: Unlike CNS neuroblasts, which rely on a special extrinsic factor (the glial-derived Jeb) to sustain neurogenesis, PNS neurons possess a unique intrinsic genetic program that endows them the resistance to nutrient stress.
claims.source: Second, unlike CNS neuroblasts, which rely on a special extrinsic factor (the glial-derived Jeb) to sustain neurogenesis, PNS neurons possess a unique intrinsic genetic program that endows them the resistance to nutrient stress.
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation based on the study's findings about FoxO expression and autophagy regulation.

claims.claim: The CNS sparing is independent of InR and Tor, made possible by the alternative Jeb/Alk/PI3K pathway, while the PNS protection still relies on InR/Tor signaling.

claims.evidence: This claim contrasts mechanisms of CNS and PNS sparing based on the study's findings and prior knowledge.

claims.claim: In the mammalian brain, FoxO members are highly expressed in NSCs and are required for the long-term maintenance of the adult NSC pool critical for adult neurogenesis.
claims.source: In the mammalian brain, FoxO members are highly expressed in NSCs and are required for the long-term maintenance of the adult NSC pool critical for adult neurogenesis (Paik et al., 2009; Renault et al., 2009; Yeo et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Paik et al., 2009; Renault et al., 2009; Yeo et al., 2013.

claims.claim: FoxOs were found to regulate dendrite branching and spine density of adult-born hippocampal neurons.
claims.source: Recently, FoxOs were also found to regulate dendrite branching and spine density of adult-born hippocampal neurons (Schäffner et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Schäffner et al., 2018.

claims.claim: FoxOs in adult-born hippocampal neurons suppress mTor signaling and maintain a level of autophagic flux that is necessary for the normal morphogenesis of the neurons.
claims.source: Interestingly, FoxOs in these neurons suppress mTor signaling and maintain a level of autophagic flux that is necessary for the normal morphogenesis of the neurons.
claims.evidence: This is a statement about findings from prior research on FoxO function in neurons.

claims.claim: FoxOs were found to be upregulated in aged brains and function to delay aging‐related axonal tract degeneration by suppressing mTor activity.
claims.source: In addition, FoxOs were found to be upregulated in aged brains and function to delay aging‐related axonal tract degeneration by suppressing mTor activity (Hwang et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Hwang et al., 2018.

claims.claim: In Drosophila C4da neurons, FoxO was previously found to promote dendrite space-filling and to mediate polyQ-induced neuronal toxicity.

results.result: Under nutrient restriction (LY), C4da sensory neurons exhibit preferential dendrite growth compared to epidermal cells, resulting in dendrite overgrowth. While LY delays overall larval development (264 hr vs 120 hr to pupariation), C4da neurons ultimately achieve 1.39-fold longer dendrites and grow 57% faster when normalized by segment width, with consistently higher dendrite density throughout development.
results.evaluation: Claims C3, C4, C29-C38, C86, and C120 collectively demonstrate preferential dendrite growth under nutrient stress through multiple complementary measurements (total length, normalized length, dendrite density, branch numbers). The data include time-course analyses, quantitative morphometric measurements with appropriate statistical analyses (R² values >0.9), and controls comparing HY vs LY conditions. The finding is internally consistent across multiple metrics and developmental timepoints.

results.result: Neuronal InR/Tor signaling mediates preferential dendrite growth under nutrient stress. Genetic manipulations (InR/Tor knockdown or dominant-negative expression) have nutrient-dependent effects: mild or non-significant effects in HY but pronounced dendrite reduction in LY. pRpS6 staining reveals that nutrient stress switches the relative Tor signaling strength, with neurons maintaining higher activity than epidermal cells under LY conditions.
results.evaluation: Claims C39-C41 and C87-C92 provide converging genetic and biochemical evidence. The genetic manipulations show statistically significant nutrient-dependent effects (interaction terms p<0.01), and pRpS6 immunostaining provides direct readout of Tor activity showing reversed ratios between neurons and epidermis under LY. The two-way ANOVA analyses appropriately test for nutrient-dependent effects. Epidermal InR/Tor suppression causing dendrite overgrowth (C87-C88) provides additional support for the relative signaling model.

results.result: C4da neurons maintain low, nutrient-independent autophagy levels while epidermal cells show robust autophagy induction under nutrient stress. Autophagosome levels (mCherry-Atg8a) in epidermal cells increase 5-fold in LY, while neuronal levels remain low in both conditions. Atg8a knockdown increases epidermal cell size by 16% in LY but has similar mild effects (11-13%) on dendrite length in both HY and LY. Mitf overexpression in neurons strongly reduces dendrite length in LY, confirming that high autophagy suppresses dendrite growth.
results.evaluation: Claims C42-C44 and C93-C103 provide comprehensive evidence through multiple autophagy markers (mCherry-Atg8a, Lamp-mCherry, GFP-mCherry-Atg8a flux reporter) and genetic manipulations (Atg8a knockdown, Mitf overexpression). The differential regulation is demonstrated with appropriate quantification and statistics. The lack of Mitf-GFPnls detection in neurons (C45, C101) provides mechanistic insight. The functional consequences are tested through loss- and gain-of-function experiments with consistent results.

results.result: FoxO is differentially expressed in neurons versus epidermal cells, with neurons showing minimal FoxO expression while epidermal cells express FoxO at high levels. Multiple reporters (FoxO-GFP, anti-FoxO antibody, foxo-Gal4) consistently show low/undetectable FoxO in C4da neurons but robust expression in epidermis. FoxO knockdown in neurons has no effect on dendrite length but knockdown in epidermis increases cell size by 34% under LY. FoxO overexpression in neurons causes nutrient-dependent dendrite reduction (11.7% in HY, 49.2% in LY).
results.evaluation: Claims C5, C47-C55, C104-C110, C121-C122, C125, and C127 provide convergent evidence from multiple independent approaches (three different FoxO reporters, immunostaining, genetic manipulations). The differential expression is consistently demonstrated across methods. The functional studies show appropriate tissue-specific and nutrient-dependent effects with statistical support. The foxo-Gal4 line was generated using the Trojan-MiMIC system to ensure endogenous regulation, strengthening the expression data. The gain-of-function experiments showing nutrient-dependent effects of FoxO overexpression support the model.

results.result: FoxO overexpression suppresses dendritic Tor signaling and induces autophagy in a nutrient-dependent manner. In HY, neuronal FoxO overexpression does not alter pRpS6 ratios, but in LY it specifically reduces dendritic (but not somatic) pRpS6 to levels below epidermal cells. Autophagosome levels in FoxO-overexpressing neurons increase 4.9-fold in LY but not in HY.
results.evaluation: Claims C56-C58 and C112-C114 demonstrate the mechanism by which FoxO overexpression affects dendrite growth through pRpS6 immunostaining and mCherry-Atg8a quantification. The compartment-specific effects (dendrites vs soma) and nutrient-dependent responses are well-documented with appropriate quantification. This mechanistically links FoxO to the Tor/autophagy axis and explains why low endogenous FoxO protects neuronal growth.

results.result: Preferential dendrite growth under nutrient stress enhances larval thermal nociception. LY larvae show increased nocifensive rolling responses across temperatures (40-46°C), with response thresholds ~2°C lower than HY larvae and more fast responses (<5s) at 43-48°C. FoxO overexpression in C4da neurons, which reduces dendrite growth in LY, significantly reduces both overall and fast responses at 46°C in LY larvae.
results.evaluation: Claims C8, C59-C62, C115-C116 provide behavioral evidence for functional consequences of dendrite overgrowth using an established thermal nociception assay. The dose-response curves across temperatures (n=90 larvae per condition) show statistically significant differences. The FoxO overexpression experiment (n=120 per group) provides a genetic link between dendrite morphology and behavior, though the authors appropriately note they cannot rule out other effects of FoxO on neuronal function (C116). The correlation between dendrite reduction and behavioral phenotype is compelling but not definitive proof of causation.

results.result: Different classes of da neurons respond differentially to nutrient stress. C1da neurons (ddaE) show no change in dendrite length under LY, while C3da neurons (ddaA, ddaF) show significant increases (32-40% total length, 46-61% terminal length, 47-58% terminal branches). All da neuron classes examined (C1da, C3da, C4da) show low FoxO expression and nutrient-independent autophagy levels, though C1da neurons uniquely show high, nutrient-responsive lysosomal markers (2.7-fold increase in LY).
results.evaluation: Claims C63-C67 and C117-C119 extend the findings to other da neuron classes with appropriate quantification. The differential responses correlate with arbor complexity and growth mechanisms (C82-C84), providing biological insight. The consistent low FoxO expression across da classes despite different growth responses suggests additional factors determine nutrient sensitivity. The C1da lysosomal data (C66) is intriguing but somewhat tangential to the main story. Sample sizes appear adequate (n=13-20) with statistical analyses performed.

results.result: PNS dendrite sparing represents a distinct form of nervous system protection from CNS brain sparing. Unlike CNS neuroblasts that rely on extrinsic glia-derived Jeb/Alk signaling independent of InR/Tor, PNS neurons use an intrinsic program (low FoxO expression) that maintains InR/Tor signaling under nutrient stress. This protects individual post-mitotic neurons at the level of arbor growth rather than protecting stem cell proliferation.
results.evaluation: Claims C69-C72 synthesize the current findings with prior work on CNS brain sparing (C2, C14-C15) to identify a novel mechanism. The distinctions are clearly supported: (1) post-mitotic arbor growth vs stem cell proliferation, (2) intrinsic genetic program vs extrinsic factor, (3) InR/Tor-dependent vs InR/Tor-independent. This represents an important conceptual advance in understanding neural protection mechanisms, though the comparison relies partly on prior literature.

results.result: Low FoxO expression confers nutrient insensitivity to neurons, giving them a growth advantage over tissues with higher FoxO expression. This FoxO-dosage-dependent nutrient insensitivity has been previously described in adult genitalia, where genital arches (low FoxO) are less affected by poor diet than wings and maxillary palps (higher FoxO).
results.evaluation: Claims C78-C80 and C111 synthesize the mechanistic findings and place them in broader context. The current data strongly support the FoxO dosage model through expression studies and gain/loss-of-function experiments. The comparison to adult genitalia (C79-C80, citing Tang et al., 2011) strengthens the generality of the mechanism, though that prior work focused on cell number rather than cell size. The claim that foxo plays a more significant role than other mTor inhibitors (C111) is supported by the candidate gene screen (C42-C46, Figure 4—supplement 1), though the negative results should be interpreted cautiously given potential RNAi efficacy issues.

results.result: In epidermal cells, high nutrition elevates InR/Tor signaling and suppresses FoxO activity and autophagy leading to high growth rates, while low nutrients reduce InR/Tor signaling and activate FoxO to stimulate autophagy and slow growth. In neurons, dendritic InR/Tor signaling is not further suppressed by FoxO when systemic insulin is low due to minimal FoxO expression.
results.evaluation: Claims C123-C124 and C126 represent the integrated model supported by the collective data on Tor signaling (C89-C92), autophagy (C93-C103), and FoxO expression/function (C47-C55). This model is well-supported by the experimental evidence, though it represents an interpretation/synthesis rather than direct experimental results. The model is depicted in Figure 8 and provides a coherent framework explaining the differential growth responses.

results.result: Rheb in neurons mildly suppresses dendrite growth in high nutrition but enhances dendrite growth under nutrient stress, showing nutrient-dependent effects (11% increase in HY, 11% reduction in LY upon knockdown).
results.evaluation: Claim C128 describes an interesting nutrient-dependent role for Rheb, but the effects are modest (11% in each direction) and the mechanism is unclear. The authors note uncertainty about whether effects are Tor-mediated. The RNAi line is validated (Francis and Ghabrial, 2015), but the biological significance of these small, opposing effects is uncertain. This finding warrants further investigation but is not well-integrated into the main story. Sample sizes appear adequate (n=12-26) but the functional interpretation remains speculative.
